chunks: A freed slave (mawla) of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), called A'yan, accompanied me. He fell ill for some days, then recovered, then died. So I took his belongings and all that was his, and brought them to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and informed him that he had been ill for some days, then recovered, then died.

He said: That is the comfort of death. Know that there is no one who dies until God, Mighty and Majestic, restores to him his hearing, his sight, and his intellect for the bequest — whether he makes it or leaves it.

key_terms.الْوَصِيَّة: The bequest or will (wasiyya); the dying person's obligation to declare their final wishes, especially regarding debts and property
key_terms.رَاحَةُ الْمَوْتِ: The comfort/ease of death — the Imam's description of the brief recovery before death as a divine grace
key_terms.مَوْلَى: Freed slave or client (mawla); in Islamic law, one whose freedom was granted by a master, resulting in a bond of loyalty (wala') between them

ai.seo_question: Does every person regain consciousness before death to make their will according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: The narrator al-Walid ibn Sabih recounts how a freed slave (mawla) named A'yan, who was connected to Imam al-Sadiq (AS), fell ill, briefly recovered, then died. When al-Walid brought the deceased's belongings to the Imam and reported the events, the Imam explained this pattern — illness, momentary recovery, then death — as the 'comfort of death,' a divinely granted lucidity allowing the dying person to make their will (wasiyya). This hadith is foundational to Islamic bequest law, affirming that God restores the faculties of hearing, sight, and reason to every dying person as an opportunity to fulfill their obligation of making a final testament.

en.hubeali:
Al Husayn Bin Muhammad, from Moala Bin Muhammad, from Al Hassan Bin Ali, from Hamaad Bin Usman, from Al Waleed Bin Sabeeh who said, 
‘A slave of Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> called Ayn accompanied me. So he complained (of health problems) for some days, then he was cured from it, then died. So I took his belongings and came with these to Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>, and informed him<sup>asws</sup> that he had complained for a few days, then was cured, then died’.

He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘That is the comfort of the death. But, there is no one who died until Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Mighty and Majestic Restores his hearing, and his eyesight, and his mind for the bequest, (either) he takes it or leaves it’.
en.sarwar: 2. Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad has narrated from Mu‘afla’ ibn Muhammad from al-Hassan ibn Ali from af-Wafid ibn Sabih who has narrated the following: “Once a Mawla’ of abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, accompanied me (on a journey) and complained of illness for several days. Then it seemed as if he had no illness but very shortly, he died. I took his luggage to abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, and informed him (the Imam) that he complained for several days, then he seemed as if he had no illness at all, but shortly thereafter he died.

He (the Imam) said, ‘That was the comfort of death. No one dies before, Allah, most Majestic, most Glorious, returns his ears, eyes and reason for making a will, regardless of whether he makes use of that opportunity or not.’”
